en: Hm? Are you attending the coming conference too?
<Yes, I am>
<No, I'm not>
I am Claude. I have a neurology practice.
I'm in England for the conference here.
I recently published a theory, but sadly,
it has not been well received.
In my view, I merely set down facts from my
clinical experience, carefully observed
You carry yourself calmly, and you seem
intelligent. You might understand it better
than the hidebound men at the conference.
If you would care to,
do read it some time.
This is the book setting out my theory.
"Three Essays on Sexuality"?
note: Freud's Three Essays (1905); Japanese title is 'Three essays on sex', shortened from the real English title for fit

en: Yes.
I'm sure you can see how it differs
from quack psychotherapy.
Now and then I rest my mind here in the park.
But I can't help thinking about the paper
I'm preparing.
Come to think of it, I never properly
introduced myself.
I've come to England for the conference
being held here.
You spoke of "clinical experience" before.
Then you are a physician, not a scholar?
I have a neurology practice in Vienna.
I am most certainly a "doctor."
Through treating patients, I carry on my
research in neurology.
This is medicine: clinical results are vital.
So then,
why "Three Essays on Sexuality"?
What is it you treat?
I mainly treat illnesses such as hysteria
and anxiety neurosis.
A great many of these illnesses are caused
by sexual repression.
Even now, with science so advanced, I know
full well that this is a dangerous subject.
Some at the conference even laughed at it.
But science must not let its progress be
halted by the world's foolish prattle.
I have argued that hysteria is an illness
men can have too. What do you think?
Does "hystera" not mean womb?
Yes. That is why I brought clinical cases
to the conference. But those hidebound men
will not even listen.
Even something this small meets resistance.
What I mean to present next will surely
meet even greater resistance...
There's a theme I want to present in the
paper I'm writing. Hear me out a moment.
First, I suspect that besides the mind we
are normally conscious of, we have another
mind that we cannot be aware of.
This other mind we cannot be aware of
I have named "the unconscious."
And what has that to do with treating
neuroses?
This part we are not aware of is the key.
People with agoraphobia or anxiety neurosis
have no idea at all why they are that way.
But in the part we call the unconscious,
the cause is plainly written down.
By probing the unconscious and laying it
bare in the conscious mind, neurosis can be cured.

en: "I feel angry, and I don't know why," or
"I don't know why, but I must go to London"
--have you never felt anything like that?
Compulsive neuroses of this kind are cured
once the "why" is understood.
Everyone has had a similar experience.
So the unconscious exists not only in
neurotic patients but in healthy people too.
